specAnchors.text: be able to select and justify a suitable experimental technique to obtain rate data for a given reaction, including: i titration ii colorimetry iii mass change iv volume of gas evolved v other suitable technique(s) for a given reaction

primer.text: Every rate measurement leans on a property that changes as the reaction proceeds and is proportional to a concentration. This note surveys the laboratory toolkit: colorimetry for colour change, mass loss for dense gases, gas collection for volume change, and titration with quenching for concentration itself, each with its suitability limits and sketch-graph reading.

modules.title: Following rate by colour: colorimetry
modules.opening: When a reaction changes colour, a colorimeter turns that change into concentration data. Light passes through the mixture, a detector logs the intensity reaching it every few seconds, and the plotted readings trace how reactants and products move with time. Precipitates spoil the method by scattering light.
keyPoints: A colorimeter measures the amount of light passing through a solution, logged every few seconds.
The light intensity reaching the detector is related to concentration, so the plotted data represent concentration against time.
For a coloured reactant the colour intensity fades with time; the sketch graph shows intensity falling.
Colorimetry cannot follow the formation of coloured precipitates, because suspended particles scatter or block the light.

low.restatement: The colorimeter logs light intensity every few seconds; since intensity tracks concentration, the plot is a concentration-time curve, and precipitates break it.
low.analogy: Watching milk dissolve into tea through a clear mug: the clearer the view, the further the mixing has gone.
low.examPointer: Name the interference problem - scattering by suspended solid - when asked why colorimetry fails for precipitates.

medium.restatement: Absorbance and concentration walk together, so a detector reading is a concentration proxy; the method's one weakness is optical, not chemical.
medium.analogy: Headlights in fog: the denser the fog between you and the lamp, the less light arrives, and any floating debris blurs everything.
medium.examPointer: If a question shows a calibration curve, use it to convert absorbance readings into concentrations before quoting rates.

modules.title: Following rate by mass loss
modules.opening: When a reaction releases a dense gas, the escaping gas carries mass out of the vessel, and a balance records the loss. Carbon dioxide from marble and acid is the classic case; hydrogen is too light for the method to resolve.
keyPoints: When a gas escapes from a reaction vessel the total mass decreases, and the decrease can be recorded with a balance.
Calcium carbonate reacting with hydrochloric acid gives off carbon dioxide; the mass is recorded every few seconds and plotted.
Mass loss measures the amount of reactant-side material lost, so the graph reads as an amount-of-reactant against time curve.
The gas must be dense enough for a 2 or 3 decimal-place balance: carbon dioxide (Mr = 44) suits the method, hydrogen (Mr = 2) does not.

low.restatement: Gas escaping removes mass; weigh every few seconds and plot the loss - but only dense gases such as CO2 register on a normal balance.
low.analogy: A shopper standing on scales while unloading oranges: each bag carried off shows as a small drop, but unloading rice grains one by one would not register.
low.examPointer: Quote the Mr comparison - CO2 at 44 works, H2 at 2 fails - when justifying the method's limits.

medium.restatement: The balance is a concentration proxy: every gram lost is gas that has formed and left, so the falling mass curve is the reaction's progress line.
medium.analogy: An hourglass read from the empty chamber: the sand that has passed is exactly what the top has lost.
medium.examPointer: State the density condition before choosing this method in a plan question.

modules.title: Following rate by gas volume
modules.opening: Trapping a product gas and reading its volume over time is the most standard rate method. A gas syringe collects the gas directly, or an inverted measuring cylinder over water works when the gas is not water soluble. Magnesium in acid giving hydrogen is the canonical example.
keyPoints: Trapping a product gas and tracking its volume over time supplies the rate data.
Magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid to release hydrogen is the standard gas-volume example.
A gas syringe gathers the gas directly; the alternative apparatus bubbles it through water into an inverted measuring cylinder, workable whenever the gas dissolves poorly in water.
The volume measured every few seconds plots as a graph of volume against time, and the volume represents the amount of product formed.

low.restatement: Collect the gas (syringe, or inverted cylinder over water for non-soluble gases), read volume every few seconds, plot volume against time.
low.analogy: Filling a party balloon from a fizzy drink: the balloon's size tracks how much gas has escaped the bottle.
low.examPointer: The dissolved-in-water caveat is the examiner's favourite caveat - state it when choosing the inverted-cylinder option.

medium.restatement: Gas volume is the product side's ruler: each cubic centimetre collected corresponds to a fixed number of moles formed, so the volume-time curve is a product-amount curve.
medium.analogy: A milometer for gas: every turn of the wheel adds a fixed distance, and the total says how far the reaction has travelled.
medium.examPointer: Remember the volume axis reads amount of product, not reactant remaining.

modules.title: Concentration itself: titration, quenching and clock points
modules.opening: Measuring concentration during a reaction is awkward because sampling and analysing take time. Quenching freezes a sample so titration can read its concentration; otherwise the clock trick stops the timer at a visible endpoint, such as the moment sulfur hides a cross under the flask.
keyPoints: Measuring concentration changes directly is difficult because taking and analysing a sample can disturb the reaction unless it is deliberately stopped, which is called quenching.
Titration of a quenched sample gives its concentration at the moment of quenching.
It is often simpler to stop the clock at a visible point in the reaction, such as when a piece of magnesium has just dissolved.
The sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid reaction slowly forms a yellow sulfur precipitate that obscures a cross seen through the solution, giving a timing point.

low.restatement: Quench a sample, titrate it for concentration; or time a visible endpoint - the disappearing-cross reaction is the standard clock point.
low.analogy: Freezing a film of a race at chosen moments: each frozen frame (quenched sample) can be measured in comfort afterwards.
low.examPointer: Use the word quenching when a question asks how to stop a sample from continuing to react.

medium.restatement: Concentration is the quantity every rate curve secretly plots, so the most direct methods grab it: freeze the chemistry, then measure at leisure.
medium.analogy: Bookmarking pages in a melting ice sculpture: you cannot measure while it melts, so you snap-freeze a copy and read it calmly.
medium.examPointer: For the thiosulfate reaction, say what the observer sees - the cross disappearing - and what that moment means: a fixed small amount of sulfur formed.

glossary.definition: Rate measurement by logging the light intensity passing through a coloured solution.
Rate measurement by recording the mass escaping as a dense gas leaves the vessel.
Deliberately stopping a removed sample's reaction so its concentration can be titrated honestly.
A sealed barrel that traps a product gas so its volume can be read against time.
